articles.title: Fixed Deposit (FD) features and tenure options
articles.content:
Fixed deposits are a popular savings instrument offered by banks in India, providing depositors with guaranteed returns on their investment. The principal amount is protected, and interest rates remain fixed throughout the deposit tenure, offering stability against market fluctuations.

Depositors can choose tenures ranging from 7 days to 10 years, allowing flexibility to match various financial goals. Shorter tenures suit temporary parking of funds, while longer tenures are ideal for building long-term savings. Interest rates typically vary based on the deposit amount and chosen tenure period.

Fixed deposits offer two primary interest payout options. Under the cumulative option, interest is compounded quarterly and paid along with the principal at maturity, allowing the investment to grow over time through the power of compounding. Under the non-cumulative or payout option, interest is paid at regular intervals—monthly, quarterly, half-yearly, or annually—providing a steady income stream.

Most banks also provide auto-renewal facilities, where upon maturity, the deposit automatically renews for the same tenure at the prevailing interest rate unless the depositor instructs otherwise. This ensures continuity of earnings without requiring manual intervention. Depositors should review their renewal instructions periodically to take advantage of potentially higher rates. Tax implications on interest earned apply as per prevailing income tax regulations.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Premature closure of Fixed Deposits and penalty
articles.content:
Premature closure means withdrawing an FD before the maturity date originally agreed with the bank. Most banks allow premature withdrawal on ordinary term deposits, although some special or non-callable products are booked on the condition that they cannot be broken early. The request is placed through netbanking, the mobile app or a branch, and the proceeds are credited to the linked savings account.

When an FD is closed early, interest is not paid at the rate booked for the full term. Instead, the bank recalculates interest at the rate applicable for the period the money actually stayed with the bank, and then applies a penalty, commonly about 1% on that applicable rate. If the FD ran for a very short period, the amount payable may be lower than expected, so customers should ask for a closure quotation before confirming.

Auto-renewed FDs and sweep-in facilities follow the same rule for the portion withdrawn. Where only part of the money is needed, breaking a single large FD may cost more than holding several smaller ones, which is why many customers ladder their savings across tenures.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Recurring Deposit (RD) rules
articles.content:
A Recurring Deposit (RD) lets a customer save a fixed sum every month for an agreed number of months, typically anywhere from six months to ten years. The instalment amount is chosen at opening and stays the same for the whole term. Interest is compounded quarterly at the rate fixed at the time of booking, and both the principal and the accumulated interest are paid out together on the maturity date.

Instalments are usually collected through a standing instruction from the linked savings account on a chosen date each month. If an instalment is missed, the bank levies a small delayed-instalment penalty, and repeatedly missed instalments can cause the RD to be discontinued and paid out early. Customers should therefore keep enough balance in the funding account around the debit date.

An RD can be closed before maturity, in which case the interest is recalculated for the period actually run and a premature closure penalty is applied in the same way as for an FD. Interest earned on an RD is taxable and forms part of the customer's interest income for the financial year. Senior citizens are usually offered an additional rate on RDs as well.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Senior citizen deposit benefits
articles.content:
Senior citizen deposit benefits are special interest rate concessions offered by banks to customers who have attained the age of sixty years or above. These benefits are available on fixed deposits and recurring deposits, which are popular savings instruments among retirees seeking stable returns.

Under this facility, senior citizens receive an additional interest rate of fifty basis points over and above the standard deposit rates applicable to the general public. This enhanced rate is offered across all deposit tenures, whether short-term or long-term, so a senior citizen earns the benefit regardless of when the deposit matures.

To avail of these benefits, customers submit proof of age at the time of opening the deposit. Accepted documents include Aadhaar, PAN, voter identification card, passport, or any other government-issued identification that clearly displays the date of birth. Once the age proof is verified, the applicable senior citizen rate is applied automatically to new deposits and renewals.

The additional rate applies only to deposits held in the senior citizen's own name, whether singly or as the first holder of a joint deposit; a joint deposit where the senior citizen is the second holder earns the regular rate. The senior citizen benefit is a bank rate concession and is separate from the interest paid under government small-savings schemes.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: TDS on Fixed Deposit interest
articles.content:
Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) is the amount a bank withholds from FD interest and pays to the government on the depositor's behalf. TDS is deducted at 10% when a valid PAN is linked to the account, and at 20% when it is not. Deduction is triggered only when the total interest paid by the bank to a customer in a financial year crosses the threshold prescribed under income tax rules; a higher threshold applies to senior citizens, and both thresholds are revised from time to time.

Customers whose total income is below the taxable limit can ask the bank not to deduct TDS by submitting the self-declaration prescribed under the income tax rules (historically Form 15G, with Form 15H being the senior citizen version). The declaration must be given afresh every financial year, before the first interest credit, and is valid only if the conditions stated on it are met.

TDS is not the final tax. The deducted amount is reflected in the customer's Form 26AS and annual information statement and is adjusted against the tax actually payable when the return is filed; a customer with no tax liability can claim a refund. A senior citizen can additionally claim the deduction under Section 80TTB on deposit interest, subject to the ceiling in force that year. The TDS certificate and an interest certificate can be downloaded from netbanking to avoid mismatches at filing time.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Deposit insurance under DICGC
articles.content:
The Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC) is a wholly owned subsidiary of the Reserve Bank of India that protects depositors in case a bank fails. Every bank licensed to operate in India, including commercial banks, regional rural banks and cooperative banks, is required to be covered by DICGC under the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation Act, 1961. The insurance premium is paid entirely by the bank; depositors pay nothing.

Under this scheme, deposits are insured up to a maximum of five lakh rupees per depositor per bank. The five lakh limit covers principal and accrued interest together and applies to the total of all deposits a customer holds in the same right and capacity with one bank, whether in savings, current, fixed or recurring deposit accounts. Money held with different banks is insured separately, and amounts held in a different capacity (for example, as a partner of a firm or as a guardian of a minor) are counted separately as well.

If a bank becomes unable to meet its obligations and is placed under liquidation or restrictions, DICGC pays the insured amount to the depositors within the period laid down in the Act. Certain balances are outside the cover: deposits of foreign governments, deposits of central and state governments, inter-bank deposits, and any amount already set off against a loan or lien-marked to the bank. A depositor's covering position can be checked by adding up all the amounts held with a single bank.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Nomination facility for deposits
articles.content:
The nomination facility lets a customer name one person who will receive the balance in a deposit, savings or current account, or the contents of a locker, when the account holder dies. It is a simple settlement mechanism: the bank can release the money to the nominee against proof of death and identity, without waiting for a succession certificate or probate. The nominee receives the funds as a trustee for the legal heirs; nomination does not by itself decide who ultimately owns the money.

Nomination is made on the prescribed form at the time of opening the account or deposit, and a nomination can be changed or cancelled later by filing the corresponding form through the branch or, where offered, through netbanking. Only one person can be nominated per deposit or account, and a minor can be nominated provided an adult is named to receive the money on the minor's behalf. The bank records the nomination in its books and mentions it on the passbook or deposit receipt.

Customers are encouraged to nominate for every deposit and account they hold, and to review the nominee after life events such as marriage or the death of a family member. Where no nominee exists, the balance is paid to the legal heirs after the bank completes its claim settlement process, which usually takes longer and needs more paperwork.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Home loan eligibility and documentation
articles.content:
Banks and housing finance companies offer home loans to both salaried and self-employed individuals who meet certain criteria. Eligibility is assessed on the applicant's income, age, employment stability and credit history. Salaried applicants are generally expected to have a minimum number of years of work experience, while self-employed applicants must show consistent business income through income tax returns and financial statements. A healthy credit score improves the chance of approval and can influence the rate offered. The eligible amount is worked out so that the proposed EMI, together with existing obligations, stays within a prudent share of monthly income, and the loan cannot exceed the loan-to-value ceiling set by the regulator for the property price band.

Documentation includes proof of identity and address such as PAN and Aadhaar, recent photographs, and income proof. Salaried applicants submit salary slips and Form 16 or Form 26AS; self-employed applicants provide income tax returns with computation of income and, where applicable, audited balance sheets. Property documents such as the agreement for sale, the approved plan and the chain of title are required because the home is mortgaged to the lender.

Most home loans are offered on a floating rate linked to an external benchmark such as the policy repo rate, with a spread that stays fixed for the life of the loan. The rate, and therefore the EMI or the tenure, changes when the benchmark is reset. A fixed-rate option is sometimes available at a higher rate. Borrowers should compare the benchmark, the spread and the processing charges rather than the headline rate alone.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Home loan prepayment and foreclosure
articles.content:
When a borrower repays a home loan partially or fully before the end of the agreed loan tenure, it is referred to as prepayment. Complete settlement of the outstanding loan amount before the tenure ends is called foreclosure. Both options allow borrowers to reduce their interest burden and become debt-free sooner.

As per Reserve Bank of India directions, banks cannot levy any prepayment penalty or foreclosure charge on home loans with a floating interest rate. This applies whether the borrower prepays part of the loan or forecloses it entirely. The protection was introduced to benefit borrowers and to promote competition among lenders.

For home loans with a fixed interest rate, the situation differs. Banks may levy prepayment or foreclosure charges since the rate remains unchanged regardless of market conditions. These charges typically compensate the lender for the interest income it forgoes when the loan is repaid early. The specific amount varies across banks and is stated in the loan agreement.

Borrowers considering prepayment or foreclosure should review their loan documents carefully. It is advisable to check whether the loan carries a floating or fixed rate, understand any applicable charges, and calculate whether early repayment offers genuine financial benefit. For part-prepayment the borrower can choose either a lower EMI or a shorter tenure; the shorter tenure saves more interest. After foreclosure the bank issues a no-dues letter for the closed loan and returns the original property documents within the regulatory timeline.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Personal loan overview
articles.content:
A personal loan is an unsecured loan granted on the strength of the applicant's income and credit history, without any collateral. It can be used for any legitimate purpose such as medical expenses, travel, education, a wedding or consolidating other debts. Because there is no security, the interest rate is higher than on a home loan or a gold loan and eligibility depends heavily on the credit score and existing repayment obligations.

Tenures usually run from 12 to 60 months and the loan is repaid in equated monthly instalments. Disbursal is quick, often within a day or two for existing customers with a pre-approved offer, since the documentation is limited to identity, address and income proof. A processing fee, commonly about 1% of the loan amount, is deducted at disbursal, and stamp duty or other statutory charges may apply.

Prepayment charges may apply on personal loans, although the regulator has restricted such charges for certain categories of borrowers, so the sanction letter should be checked for the exact terms. Customers can apply through netbanking, the mobile app or a branch, and the sanctioned amount, rate and tenure are confirmed in the sanction letter before disbursal.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Gold loan and RBI LTV cap
articles.content:
Gold loans are a secured credit facility offered by banks and non-banking financial companies in India, where borrowers pledge gold ornaments or coins to obtain funds. The Reserve Bank of India regulates the product through its lending directions, which cover valuation, the loan-to-value (LTV) ratio, auction of pledged gold and return of the ornaments after repayment.

The amount that can be borrowed is a percentage of the assessed value of the gold, known as the LTV ratio. The bank lends up to the ceiling permitted by the RBI's current LTV directions, which are tiered by loan size and revised from time to time; the ceiling is applied to the value of the gold content only, not to stones or making charges. As an illustration, if a permitted ratio of 75% applied to ornaments valued at Rs 1,00,000, the maximum loan would be Rs 75,000. The actual ratio for a given loan depends on the tier in force on the date of sanction.

One of the key advantages of a gold loan is quick processing with minimal documentation. Borrowers typically need identity proof and address proof, and the ornaments are valued at the branch by an approved assayer. Income proof is generally not required because the loan is fully secured. Interest is charged on the outstanding amount and repayment can be by EMI, by bullet payment at the end of the term, or by paying interest periodically and the principal at closure. If the value of the gold falls or the loan is not repaid, the bank issues notices before auctioning the ornaments.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: EMI, interest and amortisation basics
articles.content:
EMI, interest and amortisation basics

When a customer avails a loan from a bank, the Equated Monthly Installment or EMI is the fixed amount they pay every month until the loan is fully repaid. This amount remains constant throughout the loan tenure, combining both principal and interest components in a predetermined proportion.

In the early part of the loan tenure, a larger portion of each EMI goes toward paying interest charges while a smaller portion reduces the principal amount. As the customer progresses through the loan, this distribution shifts gradually. In later EMIs, the principal component increases and the interest component decreases. This process of gradually shifting from interest-heavy to principal-heavy payments is known as amortisation.

The total interest payable over the entire loan tenure depends on two primary factors: the rate of interest charged by the bank and the duration of the loan. A higher interest rate or a longer tenure results in greater total interest outgo. Conversely, a lower rate or shorter tenure reduces the overall interest cost. Banks calculate EMIs using a standard mathematical formula that considers the principal amount, applicable interest rate, and loan tenure.

Customers should note that part-prepayment or foreclosing the loan before the tenure ends can reduce the total interest burden, subject to the bank's terms and conditions and applicable RBI guidelines on foreclosure charges.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Loan moratorium, EMI pause and restructuring
articles.content:
Loan moratorium, EMI pause and restructuring

Customers sometimes wish to temporarily stop or reduce their Equated Monthly Instalments during financial difficulty. However, EMIs cannot be paused or skipped arbitrarily. Loan repayment schedules are contractual obligations, and missing payments without proper authorization adversely affects the customer's credit history and credit score.

When genuine financial stress arises, borrowers may approach their bank for relief under restructuring or moratorium schemes permitted by the Reserve Bank of India. These are not automatic entitlements but require a formal written request and documentation supporting the customer's hardship. Banks evaluate applications based on RBI guidelines and their internal policies before approving any relief measure.

It is important to understand that opting for a moratorium or restructuring has financial implications. While a moratorium temporarily suspends or reduces EMIs, the interest on the outstanding loan amount continues to accrue during this period. Consequently, the total interest cost over the loan's lifetime may increase, and the original tenure of the loan may be extended to accommodate the revised repayment schedule.

Customers should carefully consider these consequences and discuss all available options with their bank's customer service or relationship manager before making a decision. Proactive communication with the bank is essential to explore legitimate relief options within the regulatory framework.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: CIBIL score and its effect on loans
articles.content:
CIBIL (Credit Information Bureau India Limited) is one of the credit bureaus licensed in India that maintain credit scores for individuals based on their credit history. The CIBIL score ranges from 300 to 900, with a higher score indicating better creditworthiness. Most lenders prefer applicants with a score of 750 or above when considering loan applications.

A person's CIBIL score significantly influences both loan eligibility and the interest rate offered. Applicants with a higher score are more likely to be approved and may receive a lower rate. Conversely, a lower score can result in loan rejection, a smaller sanctioned amount, a higher rate or a demand for additional security. Credit card issuers use the score in the same way when deciding limits.

The score is built from the repayment record on existing loans and credit cards, the share of available credit limits in use, the length of credit history, the mix of secured and unsecured credit, and the number of recent enquiries. Paying every EMI and card bill on time, keeping card utilisation low and avoiding many applications in a short period improve the score over time.

Every individual is entitled to one free full credit report each year from each bureau and can dispute errors in the report online. Checking your own report is a soft enquiry and does not affect the CIBIL score.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Debit and credit card usage controls
articles.content:
Debit and credit card usage controls allow customers to manage how their cards are used across different channels and regions. Banks provide these controls to enhance security and to give customers flexibility in managing their cards.

Card controls can be applied separately for ATM withdrawals, point-of-sale transactions, online purchases and contactless payments. Customers can enable or disable each channel independently. In addition, banks distinguish between domestic transactions within India and international transactions made abroad or in foreign currency, allowing separate controls for each. Under RBI rules a newly issued card is enabled only for domestic use at ATMs and point-of-sale terminals; online, contactless and international usage must be switched on by the customer.

Customers can set daily transaction limits for each channel and region. These limits define the maximum amount that can be transacted using the card in a single day through a specific channel, and can be adjusted upward or downward subject to the bank's prescribed minimum and maximum thresholds. A credit card's overall credit limit is separate from these channel limits and is raised or lowered by the issuer on request after a review.

These controls are accessible through the bank's mobile application and netbanking portal, in the card management section, and changes take effect immediately. It is advisable to review these settings regularly; disabling channels that are not in use, and keeping international and online usage switched off until needed, reduces the exposure if card details are ever compromised.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Blocking a lost or stolen card
articles.content:
If a card is lost, stolen or suspected to be used fraudulently, it should be blocked immediately so that no further transactions can go through. Blocking can be done at any time through the bank's 24x7 helpline, the mobile app, netbanking, or by sending the designated SMS keyword from the registered mobile number. The bank confirms the block with a reference number, and the time of blocking matters because liability for later misuse rests with the bank once the customer has informed it.

A block is permanent: the blocked card cannot be reactivated. The customer should request a replacement, which is issued with a new number and delivered to the registered address, usually within a few working days; a replacement fee may apply as per the schedule of charges. Standing payments linked to the old card number need to be updated with the new details.

For a card that is merely misplaced, most banks offer a temporary freeze that switches the card off while the customer looks for it. The freeze is reversible and can be lifted from the app once the card is found, so it avoids the cost and delay of a replacement. If any unfamiliar transaction is noticed, it should be reported as a fraud dispute in addition to blocking the card.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Card fraud and unauthorised transactions
articles.content:
If you notice an unfamiliar or suspicious transaction on your card, report it to the bank immediately through the official customer service channels such as the helpline number, the mobile app or netbanking. Prompt reporting protects you from financial loss and allows the bank to block the card and secure the account. Report it even if the amount is small, because a small test transaction is often followed by larger ones.

Under Reserve Bank of India rules on customer liability, a customer has zero liability for an unauthorised transaction caused by the bank's own deficiency or by a third-party breach, provided the customer reports it within three working days of receiving the alert. If the report is made later, liability is limited to the amount prescribed for the card type, and it is unlimited only where the loss was caused by the customer's own negligence, such as sharing the PIN, OTP or card details. Once you report the matter, the bank registers it as a formal dispute and gives you a reference number.

To raise the dispute, provide the card number, the date and time of the transaction and the amount as shown in the alert, and state clearly that you did not authorise it. The bank credits the disputed amount to the account as shadow credit within ten working days and completes its investigation within the regulatory timeline, typically ninety days. You will receive the outcome in writing; if the report is not accepted you can escalate through the bank's grievance channel and then to the RBI Ombudsman. Keep transaction alerts switched on so that every debit is reported to you as it happens.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Credit card billing, minimum due and interest
articles.content:
Credit Card Billing, Minimum Due and Interest

A credit card operates on a monthly billing cycle, typically spanning 30 days, at the end of which the card issuer generates a statement summarizing all transactions, payments, and other charges. The statement displays a payment due date, usually set around 20 to 25 days after the statement generation date, giving you time to arrange payment.

The statement shows the total amount owed and a minimum amount due, which is usually a small percentage of the total outstanding balance plus any interest accrued, fees, and EMIs converted to minimum due. Paying only this minimum amount keeps your account active but does not eliminate the remaining balance.

When you carry forward any unpaid amount beyond the due date, the issuer charges interest on the outstanding balance from the date of each transaction. This interest applies even to new purchases until the previous outstanding is cleared in full. The most effective way to avoid interest charges entirely is to pay the total outstanding amount by the due date every month.

Many issuers offer an EMI conversion facility, allowing you to convert large transactions or existing balances into equated monthly installments at applicable interest rates. While this reduces monthly outgo, interest continues to apply until the EMI is fully repaid. Reviewing your statement regularly helps you track spending and plan payments accordingly.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: UPI limits and safety
articles.content:
UPI limits and safety are important aspects of digital payments that every user should understand. The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) has set a default daily transaction limit of one lakh rupees for most UPI payments, though individual banks may impose lower limits based on customer risk profiles and account history. Users should check with their bank to confirm the specific limits applicable to their account.

The most critical safety rule is never to share your UPI PIN, password, or OTP with anyone, including bank officials. Banks will never ask for these details over phone calls or messages. Scammers often impersonate bank representatives or create fake scenarios to extract this information. If you receive an unsolicited call requesting such details, disconnect immediately and report it to your bank.

Collect-request frauds are a common threat where fraudsters send payment collection requests to your UPI ID or phone number, hoping you will accidentally approve a debit instead of a credit. Always verify the purpose of any collect request before authorizing. Never respond to unknown or suspicious payment requests.

If you encounter an unauthorized transaction or dispute a UPI payment, you should immediately contact your bank through its official customer service channels and file a written complaint. You can also escalate the matter through the bank's grievance redressal mechanism or approach the Banking Ombudsman for resolution.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: NEFT, RTGS and IMPS differences
articles.content:
NEFT, RTGS and IMPS are three electronic fund transfer systems that enable customers to move money between bank accounts in India. NEFT and RTGS are operated by the Reserve Bank of India, while IMPS is operated by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI).

NEFT operates in half-hourly batches throughout the day and night, including holidays, making it convenient for customers who need flexibility in timing. There is no minimum amount limit for NEFT transactions, though there may be a maximum ceiling depending on the bank's policy. Banks generally levy a small fee that varies based on the transaction amount.

RTGS is designed for high-value transactions and processes transfers on a real-time basis without batching. As per RBI guidelines, the minimum amount for RTGS is two lakh rupees, and there is no upper limit. Because of the immediate nature of the settlement, RTGS is suitable for time-sensitive and large-value payments such as business transactions, property purchases or investment settlements. Banks typically charge higher fees for RTGS compared to other modes.

IMPS provides instant fund transfer facility available round the clock on all days including holidays. It supports both mobile and internet banking channels and works for amounts as low as one rupee up to a defined daily limit. Charges for IMPS are generally lower than RTGS and competitive with NEFT.

Customers should choose the appropriate mode based on their urgency, amount and cost preferences.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Failed transactions and auto-reversal (TAT)
articles.content:
When a payment transaction fails after the customer's account has been debited, the bank is required to reverse the amount automatically within the Turn Around Time (TAT) specified by the Reserve Bank of India. This requirement applies across channels including ATMs, UPI, IMPS, NEFT, card payments at point-of-sale and online, and wallet loads.

The RBI has harmonised the reversal timelines so that customers are treated consistently. For most failed transactions the amount must be credited back within a defined number of days from the transaction date: for example, a failed ATM cash withdrawal or a failed card or UPI payment that debits the account must be reversed by the next working day (T+1), and a failed IMPS or NEFT transfer must be reversed or credited to the beneficiary within the same short window. The exact timeline depends on the transaction type and the channel, but the framework sets clear benchmarks that banks must follow.

If the bank does not reverse the failed transaction within the stipulated TAT, the customer is entitled to compensation of one hundred rupees per day of delay beyond the prescribed timeline. This compensation is credited automatically to the customer's account and does not require a separate request; a customer who has not received it can ask for it with the transaction reference.

Customers who notice that a failed debit has not been reversed within the expected time should contact the bank with the date, amount and reference number. The bank must acknowledge the complaint and resolve it within the regulatory timelines, and the customer can escalate to the RBI Ombudsman if it is not resolved within 30 days.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Stop payment of cheques
articles.content:
A stop-payment instruction asks the bank not to honour a cheque the customer has already issued. It is used when a cheque is lost, stolen or issued in error, or when a dispute with the payee arises before the cheque is presented. The request can be placed through netbanking, the mobile app, the helpline or in writing at the branch, quoting the cheque number, date, amount and payee name, and the bank records it against the account with a reference number.

A stop payment can apply only to a cheque that has not yet been cleared. Once a cheque has been paid and the amount debited, the transaction cannot be reversed by the bank, and any recovery has to be pursued directly with the payee. Stop payment on a cheque issued towards a legitimate debt can also expose the drawer to a dishonour complaint, so it should be used for genuine reasons.

Charges may apply for each stop-payment instruction as per the schedule of charges, although many banks waive the fee when a whole cheque book is reported lost. The customer should also consider whether a fresh cheque or an electronic transfer is needed for the underlying payment, and should inform the payee that the original instrument will not be honoured.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Cheque bounce and its consequences
articles.content:
Cheque bounce and its consequences

When a cheque presented for payment is returned unpaid by the bank, it is said to have bounced. Two of the most common reasons for cheque bounce are insufficient funds in the drawer's account and mismatch between the signature on the cheque and the specimen signature held by the bank. Other reasons may include irregularities in the cheque format, posting errors, or crossing restrictions not being followed.

From the bank's perspective, bouncing a cheque attracts certain charges that vary from one institution to another. These charges are typically levied on the account holder whose cheque was returned and are disclosed in the bank's schedule of charges. The drawer may also face restrictions on issuing further cheques if bounce incidents become frequent.

Beyond financial penalties, cheque bounce carries legal consequences under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. If a cheque issued in discharge of a debt or liability is returned due to insufficient funds, the payee (or holder in due course) may initiate legal proceedings against the drawer; the drawee is the bank on which the cheque is drawn. The payee must provide written notice to the drawer within 30 days of receiving intimation of the bounce. If the amount is not repaid within 15 days of receiving such notice, the drawer may face prosecution, which can result in monetary penalty, imprisonment for a term extending up to two years, or both. It is advisable to maintain adequate balance and verify all details before issuing a cheque to avoid these consequences.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: e-Mandate, NACH and UPI AutoPay
articles.content:
An e-mandate is a standing authorisation that allows a merchant, lender or insurer to pull a recurring payment from a customer's account on a schedule. In India these recurring debits run on three main rails: NACH (National Automated Clearing House), operated by NPCI for bank-account debits such as loan EMIs and SIPs; e-mandates on debit and credit cards for subscriptions; and UPI AutoPay for recurring payments on UPI. The mandate is registered once, with the customer's authentication, and states the amount or maximum amount, the frequency and the validity period.

Under RBI rules, the bank must send a pre-debit notification before each recurring debit, and any debit above the prescribed limit needs the customer's additional authentication. Customers can view all active mandates in netbanking or the UPI app, and can pause, modify or cancel a mandate from there or by writing to the bank. Cancellation stops future debits from the date it is processed.

Cancelling a mandate does not undo money already collected: already-processed debits must be disputed separately, either with the merchant or through the bank's dispute process if the debit was not as per the mandate. Customers should also close the underlying arrangement with the merchant, otherwise the merchant may present a fresh mandate request.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: KYC and periodic re-KYC requirements
articles.content:
Know Your Customer is the mandatory verification process that every bank must carry out under the Reserve Bank of India's directions before opening an account and at intervals thereafter. At the time of opening, the customer establishes identity and address with an officially valid document such as Aadhaar, passport, driving licence, voter identity card or NREGA job card, together with PAN or Form 60. Verification may be done in person at the branch, through Aadhaar-based e-verification, or by video identification.

Periodic re-verification is required so that the bank's records stay current. The interval depends on the risk category assigned to the customer: high-risk customers are reviewed most frequently, medium-risk customers less often, and low-risk customers at the longest interval, in line with the regulator's schedule. If nothing has changed, the customer can simply give a self-declaration through netbanking, the mobile app, email from the registered address or at the branch; a fresh proof is needed only when the address or other particulars have changed.

The bank sends reminders before the due date. If the exercise is not completed in time, the bank may restrict the account and eventually freeze it for debits until the customer completes the process. Restoring the account after a freeze only requires the pending verification; no charges are levied for the exercise itself.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Types of savings and current accounts
articles.content:
Indian banks offer two primary categories of deposit accounts: savings accounts and current accounts, each designed for different customer needs.

A savings account is intended for individuals and allows them to deposit money while earning interest on the balance. Savings accounts are designed to encourage a saving habit and come with a debit card, netbanking and mobile banking, and a limited number of free transactions. The interest rate on savings accounts is set by each bank and reviewed periodically in accordance with RBI guidelines. Variants include regular savings accounts, salary accounts, senior citizen accounts, minor accounts operated by a guardian, and joint accounts.

A current account is primarily meant for business entities, traders and professionals who conduct frequent and high-volume transactions. Current accounts do not earn interest and usually allow unlimited transactions, overdraft facilities and immediate fund transfers, which supports day-to-day business operations. Most savings and current accounts require a minimum average balance, and failure to maintain it may attract charges.

The RBI mandates that all banks offer a Basic Savings Bank Deposit Account, commonly known as BSBDA, with zero minimum balance and a basic set of free services, including a debit card and a set number of free withdrawals. Small accounts with simplified verification are also available for individuals without full documents, subject to balance and transaction limits.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Minimum balance and non-maintenance charges
articles.content:
Minimum Balance and Non-Maintenance Charges

In India, banks offer various types of savings accounts, and the average monthly balance (AMB) requirement depends largely on the account variant and the location of the branch. Urban and metro branches typically have higher minimum balance requirements compared to semi-urban and rural branches. Premium or specialized account variants often carry higher thresholds than basic savings accounts. Customers should check with their bank to understand the specific AMB requirement applicable to their account and branch category.

When a customer fails to maintain the required average monthly balance, banks levy non-maintenance charges. These charges vary from one bank to another and are generally calculated based on the shortfall between the required balance and the actual average balance maintained. The charges may be fixed or linked to the extent of the shortfall. Banks usually provide a grace period or allow a certain number of instances before levying penalties.

The Basic Savings Bank Deposit Account (BSBDA), introduced by the Reserve Bank of India, is a simplified account with no minimum balance requirement. This account ensures basic banking access to all citizens, particularly those from underserved communities. BSBDA holders can avail limited transactions free of charge, with nominal fees applicable beyond the prescribed limits. Customers seeking to avoid non-maintenance charges may consider opening a BSBDA after assessing their banking needs.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Updating address and contact details
articles.content:
Updating Address and Contact Details

Customers may need to update their address or contact information stored with the bank due to relocation or change in communication preferences. The process ensures that the bank's records remain accurate and that the customer continues to receive important communications including account statements, alerts, and regulatory notifications.

To initiate an address change, customers must submit a written request along with valid proof of address. Acceptable documents typically include Aadhaar card, voter ID, passport, driving licence, or utility bills from the past three months. For contact number updates, customers may be required to provide identity verification through existing registered details or in-person authentication at a branch.

The bank will log the request in its system and verify the submitted documents through standard procedures. Address verification may involve physical verification by bank personnel or validation against official records. The requested change becomes effective only after the bank completes its verification process and confirms the authenticity of the submitted documents.

Customers should note that until verification is complete, the existing address and contact details on the bank's records will remain active. It is advisable to maintain both old and new contact information accessible during the transition period. Any discrepancy found during verification may result in delay or rejection of the request, in which case the customer will be informed of the reason and the steps needed to resolve the issue.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Dormant and inactive accounts
articles.content:
In Indian banking, a savings or current account that has recorded no customer-initiated transaction for a long period is classified as inoperative. Under the Reserve Bank of India's directions, an account becomes inoperative when there has been no customer-induced transaction for a period of two years; interest credits and bank charges do not count as customer transactions. This bank additionally applies an internal "inactive" flag after twelve months without customer activity, which triggers a reminder to the customer but does not by itself restrict the account. The word dormant is commonly used for the inoperative status.

Once an account is inoperative, debits through netbanking, cards, cheques and standing instructions are restricted, although credits such as interest, dividends and pension continue to be accepted and interest continues to be paid on savings balances. The bank does not levy charges for non-maintenance of minimum balance on an inoperative account, and reactivation is free of charge.

Reactivation requires the account holder to submit a request with fresh identity and address proof if the KYC on record is out of date, at the branch or through video verification where offered, after which the account is restored within the regulatory timeline and a fresh transaction can be carried out. Balances left inoperative for ten years are transferred to the RBI's Depositor Education and Awareness Fund but can still be claimed from the bank at any later time.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Duplicate account statements
articles.content:
Duplicate account statements are certified copies of your account transaction history for a specific period, issued by the bank upon customer request. These documents serve as official proof of your banking transactions and are commonly required for visa applications, income tax assessments, financial audits, rental agreements, and loan processing. Banks typically provide duplicate statements with the branch seal and authorized signatory to ensure they are accepted as valid supporting documents by embassies, employers, and landlords.

You can request duplicate statements through multiple channels. Most banks offer an online request facility through their internet banking portal or mobile application, where you can specify the desired date range and choose to receive the statement via email or download it as a PDF. Alternatively, you may visit your home branch with a written request or submit the request through the bank's customer service helpline. Some banks may charge a nominal fee for this service, particularly for older statements or multiple copies.

Processing time varies depending on the request method and the period covered, but digital requests are typically fulfilled within a few hours while branch requests may take one to two working days. The bank will verify your identity before processing the request to protect your account security.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Interest certificate for FD/loan
articles.content:
An interest certificate is an official document issued by the bank that summarises the interest earned on fixed deposits or the interest paid on loans during a specific period, usually a financial year. It serves as a key document for income tax filing, because taxpayers must report interest income and can claim deductions on interest paid on certain loans.

For deposit holders, the bank provides a consolidated statement showing the total interest credited across all FD, RD and savings accounts held by the customer during the year, along with the customer's PAN, the bank's TAN and the tax deducted at source, if any. Where TDS has been deducted, Form 16A is issued separately and shows the TDS amount deposited with the government.

For loan account holders, the certificate lists the total interest portion and the total principal portion of the EMIs paid during the year. This split is essential for a home loan borrower claiming the deduction on interest under Section 24 and on principal under Section 80C, and for an education loan borrower claiming the deduction under Section 80E. A provisional certificate for the current year is available in advance for submitting investment proofs to an employer.

The certificate can be downloaded free of charge from netbanking or the mobile app for the selected financial year, or requested at the branch. Details on the certificate should be checked against the annual information statement before filing.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Public Provident Fund (PPF)
articles.content:
The Public Provident Fund is a long-term savings scheme backed by the Government of India, designed to encourage small savings and provide retirement security. An account can be opened by a resident individual, including on behalf of a minor, at designated bank branches or post offices, and one person may hold only one account in their own name.

The standard tenure is fifteen years from the end of the year of opening, and it can be extended in blocks of five years, with or without further contributions, by applying within a year of maturity. The interest rate is notified by the government every quarter and is credited annually.

PPF enjoys EEE (Exempt-Exempt-Exempt) tax treatment: contributions qualify for deduction under Section 80C of the Income Tax Act, the interest earned is exempt, and the maturity proceeds are tax-free. The annual deposit limit is one lakh fifty thousand rupees per financial year across all accounts held by an individual (including a minor's account), and a small minimum deposit is required each year to keep the account active. The balance is also protected from attachment under a court decree.

Liquidity before maturity is limited. A loan against the balance is available from the third to the sixth financial year, and one partial withdrawal a year is permitted from the seventh financial year onward, subject to a cap linked to the balance in earlier years. Premature closure of the whole account is allowed only after five years and only for specified reasons such as serious illness or higher education, at a reduced rate of interest.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana (SSY)
articles.content:
Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana (SSY) is a small deposit savings scheme launched by the Government of India specifically for the welfare of the girl child. The scheme encourages parents and guardians to build a financial corpus for their daughter's future needs, including education and marriage expenses.

To open an SSY account, the girl child must be below ten years of age. Only two accounts can be opened per family, with a maximum of one account per girl child. The account can be opened at any post office or authorised bank branch by submitting the required documents, including the girl's birth certificate and identity proofs of the guardian.

The scheme offers an attractive rate of interest that is compounded annually, making it one of the highest-yielding small savings instruments available in the country. Deposits need to be made for a period of fifteen years from the date of account opening. The minimum and maximum deposit limits are set by the government and may be revised periodically.

One of the significant advantages of SSY is the tax benefit it offers under Section 80C of the Income Tax Act, 1961. Contributions made towards the scheme are eligible for deduction from taxable income, subject to the prescribed limits.

The account matures when the girl child attains twenty-one years of age. Upon maturity, the accumulated balance including the interest earned is payable to the account holder.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Senior Citizens Savings Scheme (SCSS)
articles.content:
The Senior Citizens Savings Scheme (SCSS) is a government-backed savings instrument designed to provide regular income and tax benefits to senior citizens. It is available at designated banks and post offices across the country.

To be eligible for SCSS, an individual must have attained the age of 60 years or above. Those who have retired under a voluntary retirement scheme or superannuation scheme can open an account at the age of 55 years, provided the investment is made within one month of receiving the retirement benefits. Non-resident Indians are not eligible to open SCSS accounts.

The scheme has a tenure of five years, which can be extended for an additional three years by submitting Form B within one year of maturity. The maximum amount that can be deposited under SCSS is Rs 30 lakh, calculated on the basis of the date of deposit and the age of the account holder.

Interest on SCSS deposits is paid out on a quarterly basis, and the rate is revised quarterly by the government. The interest earned is taxable as per the investor's income tax slab. However, the investment qualifies for deduction under Section 80C of the Income Tax Act, up to the specified limit.

Premature withdrawal is permitted, subject to a penalty. On the death of the account holder, the balance is paid to the nominee.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Atal Pension Yojana (APY)
articles.content:
Atal Pension Yojana (APY) is a government-backed pension scheme designed specifically for workers in the unorganised sector who do not have any formal pension coverage. The scheme was launched to provide financial security during retirement years.

Eligibility and Enrollment

Indian citizens aged between 18 and 40 years can enroll in APY through their bank account. Since pension benefits begin only from age 60, subscribers must continue contributing for a minimum period that enables adequate accumulation. Those already covered under statutory social security schemes such as EPF, NPS, or employees' state insurance are generally not eligible.

Pension Benefits

Under APY, subscribers receive a guaranteed minimum pension ranging from Rs 1,000 to Rs 5,000 per month after attaining 60 years of age. The actual pension amount depends on the contribution made during the accumulation period. Spouses of deceased subscribers are entitled to continue receiving the pension amount.

Contribution and Auto-Debit

Contributions are regularly auto-debited from the subscriber's linked bank account on a monthly, quarterly, or half-yearly basis as per the chosen frequency. The amount is fixed at the time of enrollment and remains unchanged throughout the contribution period. Subscribers should maintain sufficient balance to avoid missed contributions, which could affect eventual pension eligibility.

The scheme is administered by the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority. Income-tax payers are not eligible to enrol.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: PM Jeevan Jyoti and Suraksha Bima (PMJJBY/PMSBY)
articles.content:
Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana (PMJJBY) and Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana (PMSBY) are two low-cost insurance schemes of the Government of India that are distributed through bank accounts. Both are renewable one-year covers running from 1 June to 31 May, and the annual premium is auto-debited from the subscriber's savings account each year on the basis of a standing consent given at enrolment.

PMJJBY is a term life insurance cover for bank account holders aged 18 to 50 years. It pays a fixed sum assured to the nominee on the death of the insured from any cause, and the cover can continue until the subscriber turns 55 provided the premium keeps being paid. Claims are settled by the partner life insurer through the bank.

PMSBY is an accident insurance cover for account holders aged 18 to 70 years. It pays the full sum assured for accidental death or total permanent disability and half the sum for partial permanent disability. The premium is nominal, and a person may hold each cover through only one bank account.

Enrolment is done through netbanking, the mobile app, a branch or a business correspondent by giving the auto-debit consent and nominee details. The cover lapses if the account is closed or does not have enough balance for the premium on the debit date, and it can be re-joined later by paying the premium and, for PMJJBY, giving a good-health declaration.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY)
articles.content:
Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) is a flagship financial inclusion scheme launched by the Government of India in August 2014. Its objective is to ensure universal access to banking services for every household, particularly the unbanked and underbanked segments of the population.

Under PMJDY, an eligible individual can open a basic savings account with zero balance at any branch or business correspondent outlet. The account functions like a regular savings account and lets the holder receive government benefits, subsidies and wages directly through direct benefit transfer. Simplified Know Your Customer norms allow a small account to be opened even with limited documents, subject to balance and transaction limits.

Every PMJDY account holder receives a domestic debit card that enables cash withdrawals at ATMs and purchases at point-of-sale terminals. The card carries a built-in accident insurance cover for the account holder, subject to the card having been used within the period specified under the scheme. The scheme also provides for an overdraft facility on the account after a satisfactory operation period, subject to eligibility and the bank's assessment, which gives the holder a small line of credit for emergencies.

PMJDY accounts are the channel for the associated financial inclusion covers such as PMJJBY, PMSBY and Atal Pension Yojana, and they carry no minimum balance requirement or charges for basic services.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Kisan Vikas Patra and National Savings Certificate
articles.content:
Kisan Vikas Patra and National Savings Certificate are popular small savings schemes backed by the Government of India, offering safe investment options with guaranteed returns. These certificates are widely available at post offices and can also be purchased through designated banks, making them accessible to investors across urban and rural areas.

Kisan Vikas Patra is a fixed-income investment scheme where the principal amount doubles over a specific maturity period. The interest earned is compounded annually and added to the maturity value. The tenure and applicable interest rates are notified by the government periodically and remain fixed for the duration of the investment.

National Savings Certificate carries a fixed interest rate that is compounded half-yearly. The certificate has a fixed maturity period, and investors receive the accumulated amount upon completion of the tenure. One of the key advantages of NSC is the tax deduction available under Section 80C of the Income Tax Act, allowing investors to claim deductions on the amount invested, subject to the overall ceiling under that section.

Both schemes are considered low-risk investments suitable for conservative investors seeking stable returns. The invested amount and accrued interest are guaranteed by the government, providing a secure avenue for savings. Investors should note that premature withdrawal conditions and tax implications may vary, and it is advisable to review current government notifications before investing.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Banking services for differently-abled customers
articles.content:
Banks in India are required under Reserve Bank of India directions to make their services accessible to differently-abled customers on an equal footing with other customers, and the RBI mandate covers branches, ATMs and digital channels. Branches are expected to have ramps and step-free access, priority service at the counter, and staff trained to assist customers with visual, hearing, mobility or intellectual disabilities. A differently-abled customer can operate an account independently, and a thumb impression or a mark can be used in place of a signature with the bank's witness procedures.

ATMs are being made accessible with Braille keypads, audio guidance through an earphone jack and a lower height for wheelchair users; the location of such talking ATMs is published by each bank. Mobile apps and netbanking portals are required to be screen-reader compatible, and statements and forms can be requested in accessible formats such as large print, Braille or audio.

Customers who find it difficult to visit a branch can use doorstep banking, and a person with a disability may nominate an authorised representative to deal with the bank. Cheque books, debit cards and loans cannot be refused merely on the ground of disability. Complaints about accessibility can be raised through the regular grievance channels and escalated to the RBI Ombudsman.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Doorstep banking for senior citizens and disabled
articles.content:
Many banks in India offer doorstep banking services specifically designed for senior citizens aged 70 years and above, as well as differently-abled customers who may find it difficult to visit branches. Under RBI directions, banks must make these services available on request, and they support the wider goal of keeping banking accessible for senior citizens and disabled customers.

Doorstep services typically include cash delivery against a withdrawal request, cash pickup for deposit, cheque pickup for collection, delivery of demand drafts and account statements, and collection of forms such as a life certificate or a KYC update. A bank representative visits the registered address on the scheduled date, which is convenient for senior citizens living alone, verifies the customer's identity and completes the transaction, subject to per-visit cash limits and a nominal per-visit charge listed in the schedule of charges.

For customers unable to complete verification at a branch, banks offer doorstep verification. An authorised representative may visit to record identity details, collect photographs and obtain documents, and some banks facilitate Aadhaar-based e-KYC updates at the customer's home.

To request doorstep services, senior citizens and disabled customers can call the bank's dedicated helpline, visit the nearest branch, or place a request through the website or the mobile app. A family member or caregiver may make the request on the customer's behalf, but the customer must be present at the time of the visit for verification.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Braille and talking ATMs
articles.content:
Indian banks provide accessible automated teller machines designed to serve customers with visual impairments. These talking ATMs incorporate features that enable independent cash withdrawals and other transactions without assistance from bank staff.

Tactile keypads are a key feature. The numeric keys carry raised Braille numbers so that users can identify keys by touch, and function keys such as cancel, clear and enter are shaped differently from one another, making it easy to distinguish between them during operation.

Audio guidance through an earphone jack provides step-by-step voice instructions throughout the transaction. The user plugs a personal earphone into the designated port to receive audible prompts; the system announces each screen, guides the user through entering the PIN, selecting the amount and confirming the transaction, and can blank the screen so that the audio output remains private to the individual user.

To locate an accessible ATM, customers can check the ATM locator on the bank's website or mobile app, which marks talking ATMs and wheelchair-accessible sites, or ask at any branch. Banks are required to make new and replacement ATMs accessible, and a customer who finds an ATM without working audio guidance can report it through the helpline so that it is repaired.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Accessible documentation formats
articles.content:
Indian banks are required under RBI guidelines to provide accessible documentation formats for customers with visual impairments and other disabilities. If you need account statements, forms, terms and conditions, or other banking documents in large print, Braille or audio, you can request them through your bank's customer service channels or at your home branch. Banks typically process such requests within a reasonable timeframe and may ask for the request in writing to record exactly what is required.

Some banks have dedicated special needs or accessibility departments that coordinate these services, and RBI regulations also mandate that bank staff receive training to assist customers with disabilities appropriately. Digital statements and e-mails are produced so that they work with screen readers, and the mobile app and netbanking portal are expected to work with screen readers and magnification.

The availability of specific formats may vary across banks and products, and printed Braille documents may take longer to prepare than large print or audio. Once a preferred format is recorded on the customer's profile, subsequent statements and notices are issued in that format without a fresh request. There is no charge for accessible formats of documents the bank issues free of cost in the standard format.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: How to raise a complaint with the bank
articles.content:
A customer can raise a complaint with the bank through any of its service channels: at the branch in writing, on the 24x7 helpline number, through netbanking or the mobile app, by e-mail to the designated grievance address, or through the complaint form on the website. Every complaint gets a reference number at the time it is registered, and the customer should keep this number for all follow-up.

The bank works to a defined resolution TAT (turnaround time) that depends on the type of complaint; the timelines are published in the bank's grievance redressal policy, and regulatory timelines apply to failed transactions and unauthorised debits. The customer is informed of the outcome in writing, and if the complaint is rejected the reason is stated.

If the customer is not satisfied with the response or the TAT is not met, the complaint can be escalated through the escalation matrix: first to the branch head or the regional grievance officer, then to the bank's Principal Nodal Officer, whose contact details are displayed at every branch and on the website. If the bank does not resolve the complaint within 30 days of receiving it, or the customer is not satisfied with the resolution, the matter can be taken to the RBI Integrated Ombudsman free of cost.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Banking Ombudsman / RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme
articles.content:
The Reserve Bank - Integrated Ombudsman Scheme is the free grievance redressal mechanism run by the Reserve Bank of India for customers of banks, non-banking financial companies and payment system operators. It replaced the earlier Banking Ombudsman scheme and works on a "one nation, one ombudsman" basis, so a complaint can be filed without worrying about jurisdiction.

A customer can approach the Ombudsman only after first complaining to the bank. If the bank rejects the complaint, or does not reply within 30 days, or the customer is not satisfied with the reply, the complaint can be escalated to the Ombudsman within one year of the bank's reply. Deficiency in service of any kind is covered, such as unauthorised debits, delays in reversal, wrongful charges, loan servicing issues and mis-selling.

Complaints are filed online through the RBI's Complaint Management System (CMS) portal, by e-mail, or by post to the centralised receipt and processing centre, and there is a toll-free helpline for assistance. There is no fee. The Ombudsman first attempts a settlement between the customer and the bank and, failing that, passes an award that is binding on the bank if the customer accepts it. Compensation for loss of time and mental agony can also be awarded within the scheme's limits.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Disputing an unauthorised debit
articles.content:
If you notice a transaction on your account that you did not authorise, report it to the bank immediately through the helpline, the mobile app, netbanking or your home branch. When raising the dispute, provide the transaction reference number or unique identification number shown in the alert or statement, the date, the amount and the channel, as this helps the bank locate and investigate the entry quickly. The bank registers the dispute and gives you a complaint reference.

Under Reserve Bank of India guidelines, the bank must give provisional credit for the disputed amount within ten working days of receiving the report, without waiting for the investigation to conclude, and must complete the investigation within the regulatory timeline, typically ninety days. The liability conditions depend on how quickly the transaction was reported: zero liability if it was reported within three working days of the alert, a limited liability if reported within four to seven working days, and liability as per the bank's board-approved policy after that. Where the loss arose from the customer's own negligence, such as sharing the PIN or OTP, the customer bears the loss until the transaction is reported.

Zero-liability protection applies to fraud, hacking and phishing where no fault lies with the customer. If the investigation confirms that the debit was unauthorised, the provisional credit becomes permanent; if it does not, the bank must explain the reasons in writing. Keep the transaction alerts switched on and the registered mobile number current so that every debit reaches you at once, and escalate to the RBI Ombudsman if the timelines are not met.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Charges dispute and fee reversal
articles.content:
Customers who believe a charge has been wrongly levied on their account, such as a non-maintenance fee, an ATM charge, an SMS alert fee, a late payment fee on a credit card or a charge that does not appear in the schedule of charges, can dispute it and request a reversal. The request can be made through the helpline, netbanking, the mobile app or the branch, quoting the date and amount of the charge and the reason it is considered incorrect.

The bank reviews the request against the account's terms and the schedule of charges in force on the date of the debit. Where a charge was applied in error, for example a fee levied on an account variant that is exempt, or a duplicate debit, the bank reverses it, usually within a few working days, and the reversal appears as a separate credit. Where the charge was correctly applied, the bank may still consider a goodwill waiver, for instance for a first-time lapse or a long-standing customer.

Outcomes are not guaranteed: the decision to reverse or waive a correctly levied charge is subject to the bank's review and its policy, and the customer is informed of the outcome with the reasons. If the customer is not satisfied, the matter can be escalated through the bank's grievance channels and, after 30 days, to the RBI Ombudsman. Charges disclosed in the schedule and applied as per terms are generally not treated as a deficiency in service.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Bancassurance products through the bank
articles.content:
Bancassurance refers to the distribution of insurance products through a bank's branch network and digital channels. The bank acts as a corporate agent registered with the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India and offers life insurance, health insurance and general insurance products of the insurers it has tied up with. The bank facilitates the sale by providing access to its customer base and infrastructure, while the policy itself is issued and underwritten by the insurer, not by the bank.

When a customer buys a policy through the bank, the proposal form is submitted to the insurer, the premium is collected by the bank on the insurer's behalf, and the policy document is issued by the insurer. The insurer is the party responsible for the terms of the cover, premium payment schedules, policy servicing and claims. Claims are handled by the insurer; the bank can assist with forms and forwarding documents but does not decide or pay a claim.

Buying insurance is never a condition for obtaining a loan or any other banking service, and customers can decline a bundled product. Customers should read the policy wording, check that the premium and the cover match what was explained, and use the free-look period to cancel a policy that does not suit them. Complaints about mis-selling can be made to the bank and the insurer, and escalated to the respective ombudsman.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Filing an insurance claim
articles.content:
When an insured event occurs, notify the insurer as promptly as possible. Most policies require timely intimation, and delays may affect the processing of the claim or even result in rejection. Contact the insurer through its designated customer service channels, by phone, e-mail or its official website, quote the policy number and give the basic details of the incident. The insurer registers the claim and issues a claim number.

The insurer will guide you on the documents required to support the claim. Commonly needed documents include the original policy document, a duly filled claim form, identity proof of the claimant, and evidence of the loss or event such as medical records and hospital bills, repair estimates, a police report or photographs, depending on the type of insurance. For a life insurance claim the nominee submits the death certificate and proof of identity and bank account.

Once submitted, the insurer evaluates the claim against the policy terms, conducts any required assessment or investigation, and settles the claim if it is admissible, within the timelines laid down by the insurance regulator. The time taken depends on the complexity of the case and the completeness of the documents.

If the policy was bought through the bank, the bank acts as an intermediary and assists with the process by helping to fill the claim form and forwarding documents to the insurer. However, the bank does not assess, approve or pay claims; the decision rests with the insurer, and a disputed claim can be escalated to the insurer's grievance cell and then to the Insurance Ombudsman.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Insurance premium payment options
articles.content:
Insurance premium payment options

Policyholders can pay their insurance premiums through multiple channels offered by banks and insurers. One convenient option is setting up an auto-debit mandate, which authorises the insurer to automatically deduct the premium amount from the linked bank account on the due date. This eliminates the risk of accidental missed payments and ensures continuous coverage.

Net-banking facilities allow policyholders to make one-time or recurring premium payments directly through their bank's internet banking portal. This method provides flexibility in choosing payment dates and amounts.

Insurers and banks typically send payment reminders through SMS and email prior to the premium due date. These communications are sent well in advance to give policyholders sufficient time to arrange funds.

Most insurance policies include a grace period, usually ranging from fifteen to thirty days after the due date, during which the policy remains active even if the premium is not paid. Coverage continues during this period, though interest may be charged on late payments.

If the premium remains unpaid beyond the grace period, the policy lapses and coverage ceases. Policyholders can revive a lapsed policy within the stipulated revival period by paying outstanding premiums along with applicable interest and meeting health requirements specified by the insurer.

Figures are illustrative for a synthetic environment; verify current regulations.

articles.title: Safe deposit locker rules and agreement
articles.content:
When a customer hires a safe deposit locker from a bank, the relationship is governed by a locker agreement that must comply with Reserve Bank of India guidelines, most recently revised in 2021. The agreement is a contract between the bank and the locker hirer on stamp paper, in the model format recommended by the industry association, and it sets out the terms of usage, the rent, the access process and the responsibilities of both parties. Lockers are allotted on a first-come basis from a waitlist maintained at the branch, and the bank may take a fixed deposit covering a limited number of years' rent as security.

The locker rent is payable in advance at the rates notified by the bank, which must be displayed at the branch. Access is allowed only to the hirer or an authorised joint hirer after identity verification, and the bank records each visit. If rent stays unpaid for a prolonged period or the locker is unused for several years, the bank sends notices before it can break open the locker in the presence of witnesses.

Nomination facilities are available: a sole hirer or joint hirers can nominate a person who, on the hirer's death, can claim access to the locker contents by following the bank's procedure, and the contents are released within the regulatory timeline after the claim.

Regarding bank liability, the revised rules state that the bank is not responsible for loss caused by natural calamities or the customer's own negligence, but it is liable for loss caused by fire, theft, burglary, building collapse or fraud by its staff, up to one hundred times the annual locker rent. Banks must therefore exercise due care in safeguarding the locker room and maintaining its security systems.
