articles.title: Prohibited items in bank lockers
articles.content:
Prohibited items in bank lockers

Bank locker facilities are designed exclusively for the safe storage of valuables, important documents, and precious items. Certain categories of items are strictly prohibited from being stored in these lockers in accordance with regulatory guidelines and safety considerations.

Arms, ammunition, and explosives of any kind are absolutely prohibited. This includes firearms, weapons, bullets, gunpowder, and any explosive or incendiary materials. Storing such items violates not only bank policies but also various provisions under the Arms Act and Explosives Act.

Hazardous and illegal substances cannot be placed in bank lockers. This encompasses flammable chemicals, radioactive materials, toxic substances, and any items whose possession or storage is prohibited under Indian law. Banks reserve the right to inspect locker contents if there is reasonable suspicion of violation.

Perishable items including food products, plants, and organic materials that may decompose, emit odors, or attract pests are not permitted. Such items pose hygiene risks and could damage the locker facility.

Only valuables such as jewelry, precious metals, important documents like property papers and insurance policies, and items of significant personal or financial value should be stored in bank lockers. Customers are advised to maintain an inventory of contents for reference purposes.

articles.title: Mobile and net banking registration
articles.content:
Mobile and net banking registration

Most Indian banks offer multiple convenient methods to activate internet and mobile banking services. Customers can typically register through their bank's official website, mobile application, or by visiting a branch with valid identity proof.

For self-registration through online channels, customers usually require their customer ID, registered mobile number linked to their account, and their debit card details. The process involves verifying these credentials and setting up login credentials along with a confidential MPIN for mobile transactions. The MPIN serves as a secure authentication factor for authorizing payments and fund transfers initiated through mobile banking applications.

Customers who prefer in-person assistance can submit a written request at their home branch. The bank verifies the customer's identity and activates the services, after which login credentials are dispatched to the registered address or provided at the branch itself.

Transaction limits are prescribed by RBI guidelines and vary based on the type of transaction, authentication method used, and the customer's account category. Banks may impose additional daily or per-transaction limits for security purposes. Device binding, wherein the mobile application is linked to a specific mobile device, adds another layer of security and helps prevent unauthorized access from other devices. Customers are advised to notify the bank immediately if they suspect any security breach or lose their registered mobile device.

articles.title: Online banking safety and phishing
articles.content:
Online Banking Safety and Phishing

Protecting your account and personal information is essential when using digital banking services. Fraudsters often attempt to steal sensitive data through phishing emails, fake websites, and phone calls, making it vital to stay vigilant at all times.

Your bank will never ask you to share your One-Time Password, CVV, PIN, or internet banking password under any circumstances. If someone claiming to be from the bank requests this information, do not provide it and report the incident immediately through the bank's official helpline. Remember that genuine bank representatives do not need your credentials to assist you.

Phishing attempts typically arrive through emails or messages that appear to be from your bank, urging you to click on links or provide personal details. Always verify that you are on the official website by checking the URL carefully before logging in. Avoid accessing banking services through links received via SMS or email, and type your bank's website address directly into your browser.

Vishing refers to fraudulent phone calls where callers impersonate bank officials or customer service representatives. They may create a sense of urgency, claiming suspicious transactions or account issues to pressure you into sharing confidential information. Stay calm and end such calls without engaging.

Keep your devices updated, use strong passwords, and enable transaction alerts to monitor your account activity regularly. If you notice any unauthorized transactions, inform your bank immediately.

articles.title: Resetting netbanking password / MPIN
articles.content:
A customer who has forgotten the netbanking password or the MPIN used in the mobile app can reset it without visiting a branch. The self-service option on the login page asks for the customer ID or registered mobile number, verifies the customer with the debit card number and ATM PIN, and sends a one-time password to the registered mobile number and e-mail. Once the OTP is confirmed, the customer sets a new password or MPIN, and a confirmation alert is sent. Customers without an active debit card can reset through the branch by submitting a written request with identity proof, after which fresh credentials are issued.

For security, the account is locked after repeated failures: entering a wrong password or MPIN several times in succession disables the login for a period or until it is unlocked through the reset process or the helpline. This prevents guessing attacks. The bank never asks for the password, MPIN or OTP on a call or message, and a reset request that the customer did not initiate should be reported at once.

A strong password uses a mix of letters, numbers and symbols and is not reused on other sites; the MPIN should not be a date of birth or a simple sequence. Both should be changed periodically and immediately after any suspected compromise.

articles.title: Common banking service charges
articles.content:
Banks in India levy service charges for certain transactions and facilities, and these charges are disclosed in the Schedule of Charges, which is available on the bank's website and at branches. Customers are advised to review this schedule periodically as charges may be revised with notice.

Cheque book issuance typically attracts a nominal fee per leaf, with many banks offering a certain number of free cheque leaves per year depending on the account variant. For duplicate account statements, banks usually charge a fee per statement period requested, although statements downloaded from netbanking or e-mailed are generally free. SMS alerts for transactions are free for a basic package, with a nominal quarterly charge for enhanced alerts on some variants.

Debit card annual fees depend on the card type and the account category, and are often waived if the customer meets a balance or spend condition; a replacement card carries a separate fee. Cash handling charges may apply for large cash deposits or withdrawals at branches beyond a monthly free limit, with thresholds and rates varying across account types. Other common charges include those for fund transfers through some channels, demand drafts, stop-payment instructions, cheque returns, and balance certificates.

Customers should note that a Basic Savings Bank Deposit Account is exempt from most of these charges, and that charges cannot be applied without disclosure in the schedule. A charge that appears incorrect can be disputed through the bank's grievance channels.

articles.title: ATM transaction charges and free limits
articles.content:
In India, banks provide a certain number of free ATM transactions each month as per Reserve Bank of India guidelines. The exact number of free transactions depends on whether the ATM belongs to your own bank or another bank, and whether the ATM is located in a metro city or a non-metro location.

For transactions at your own bank's ATMs, customers get a set number of free transactions per month, usually five, covering both cash withdrawals and non-financial transactions such as balance enquiry and mini statement. When using ATMs of other banks, the free allowance is lower: three free transactions per month in metro cities and five in non-metro locations, because non-metro areas have fewer banking touchpoints.

Once you exceed the free monthly limit, the bank levies a charge per transaction, subject to the maximum permitted by the RBI, and the charge is disclosed in the schedule of charges. Failed transactions due to technical reasons, invalid PIN or insufficient balance are not counted against the free limit, and a failed withdrawal that debits the account must be reversed within the prescribed turnaround time.

Cash withdrawal at ATMs is also subject to a daily limit set on the card, which can be changed through the card controls in the mobile app. Customers who withdraw often can reduce charges by using their own bank's ATMs or by withdrawing larger amounts less frequently.

articles.title: NRE and NRO account differences
articles.content:
NRE (Non-Resident External) and NRO (Non-Resident Ordinary) accounts are the two rupee accounts that a Non-Resident Indian (NRI) or a Person of Indian Origin can open with a bank in India. Both are maintained in Indian rupees and can be savings, current, recurring or fixed deposit accounts, but they differ in the source of the money, its repatriability and its tax treatment. A person who becomes non-resident must re-designate existing resident accounts into one of these types.

An NRE account holds foreign earnings remitted to India from abroad. Funds are converted into rupees on credit, and both the principal and the interest are fully and freely repatriable outside India without any ceiling. Interest earned on an NRE account is exempt from income tax in India. Local rupee income cannot be credited to an NRE account, and the account can be held jointly only with another non-resident or, on a former-or-survivor basis, with a resident close relative.

An NRO account is used to manage income earned in India, such as rent, dividends, pension or the sale proceeds of property, and can also receive foreign remittances. Interest on an NRO account is taxable in India and tax is deducted at source at the applicable rate. Repatriation from an NRO account is permitted up to the annual limit prescribed under foreign exchange rules, on production of a chartered accountant's certificate and the prescribed tax forms.

Both accounts can be opened with the usual identity documents together with proof of NRI status such as a passport with visa or a residence permit, and the two accounts can be held with the same bank at the same time.

articles.title: Positive Pay System for cheques
articles.content:
The Positive Pay System (PPS) is a fraud prevention mechanism introduced by the Reserve Bank of India that requires account holders to confirm cheque details electronically before high-value cheques are cleared. When a cheque is presented through clearing, the drawee bank compares the details submitted by the issuer with the details on the instrument, so that an altered or forged cheque can be identified before it is paid.

Banks make the facility available for cheques of Rs 50,000 and above, and many banks make it mandatory for cheques of higher amounts. To use Positive Pay, the account holder submits the cheque number, cheque date, payee name and amount to the bank through netbanking, the mobile app, SMS or the branch before handing the cheque to the payee. The bank stores these details and cross-checks them when the cheque is presented for clearing.

If the details match, the cheque is paid in the normal course. If they do not match, or no details were submitted for a cheque where confirmation is mandatory, the cheque is returned unpaid and the drawer is informed, and a return charge may apply. Positive Pay applies only to cheques presented through clearing, not to cheques paid over the counter at the drawee branch, and details once submitted cannot be changed, so the cheque should be issued exactly as confirmed.

articles.title: Standing instructions for recurring payments
articles.content:
Standing instructions are automated payment instructions set up by a customer to execute recurring transfers or bill payments on specified dates without requiring manual intervention each time. They are commonly used for transfers to a family member's account, monthly deposits into an RD or a PPF account, rent, loan EMIs to another bank, credit card bill payments and utility bills. The customer chooses the amount, the frequency, the start date and the end date, and the bank executes the debit on schedule from the chosen account.

A standing instruction can be set up, modified or cancelled through netbanking, the mobile app or a written request at the branch. Changes take effect from the next scheduled date, and cancellation stops all future executions. If the account does not have sufficient balance on the due date, the instruction fails for that cycle, the bank may retry as per its policy and levy a failure charge, and the customer should make the payment manually to avoid a late fee at the receiving end.

The difference from mandates is that a standing instruction is created and controlled by the customer with the bank, for a fixed amount, whereas an e-mandate or NACH mandate is registered at the request of a merchant or lender and lets that party pull a variable amount within an agreed cap. Customers should review their active instructions periodically and cancel those no longer needed.
